caseno: Appeal From Original Order No. 75 of 1983.
lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Saleh Uddin Ahmed, Advocates ----- For the Appellant. 
Rafiqul Huq with ABM Khairul Hoque, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Adamjee Sons Limited ----- Appellant. 
Vs. 
Jiban Bima Corporation ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. Before I proceed to deliver the judgment I am impelled to make certain observation on the conduct of this case. The history in conducting this case, a luxury litigation, at the instance of the two agencies of the same Government must receive disapproval of this court. A luxury litigation, defying the decision to settle the dispute once and for all through arbitration of a very high power committee of the Government, should not be encouraged. In recording disapproval I seek support from the judgment of Blagden J, and am tempted to quote a quotation from his judgment which is "some years before the present war, and for ought I know to the contrary since a man used to stand Outside the Courts of justice in London with a banner inscribed on one side with the words" 'Arbitrate, Do not Litigate' and on the other with the words" Beware of Lawyers. "In this, regard the purpose of arbitration needs also spell out for the guidance of the litigants' and to borrow the expression of Sir John Bonaldson, Mr. Where there is a choice between arbitration and litigation, there will be a number of factors to be taken into account. The claim usually made in that arbitration is quicker, cheaper, more expert and more private than litigation If you are in the wrong and want to gain time, insist upon the best Arbitrator in the business". The reasons for which I am driven to quote the aforesaid passage are; that this case has a chequered career and has travelled a long zig-zag course through arbitration and through law court. Ultimately the parties to the disputes felt such Inter-Ministerial wrangling over the possession of Annex Building should not be allowed to continue for long and should be decided once and for all". Before approaching the law Court more so where the parties submit to the Arbitration, they must remember that they submit only to bury the dispute once and for all. 

 3. Now, I proceed to deal with the appeal. The appellant has taken in the memorandum of appeal as many as 28 grounds. In order to appreciate the contention raised at the Bar it is necessary, in nutshell, to state the facts of the case. On August 15, 1981 an agreement for arbitration was executed the preamble of which (page 10 of the Additional Paper Book) states that parties, the Adamjee Sons Limited and the Jiban Bima Corporation, agree to the reference to Arbitration of the dispute referred to in Schedule III of the agreement in terms and conditions mentioned therein. According to term No. 1 the appellant and the respondent were to refer the question of ownership and possession of the properties described in Schedule III to the arbitration of Mr. Justice TH Khan and the Award was to taka effect according to the provisions of Arbitration Act. According to term No. 4, Title Suit No. 165 of 1980 filed by the appellant against the award passed by Mr. AR Chowdhury mentioned in Schedule 1 was to be set aside on compromise and according to term No. 5 other pending suits mentioned in the Schedule III were to be withdrawn by the respective parties within 7 (seven) days. Under Schedule II falls Title Suit No. 19 of 1977 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka filed by the appellant against the Respondent. Title Suit No. 194 of 1974 of the same Court was instituted by the respondent against the appellant and two others. Under Schedule III of the Arbitration Agreement falls the properties under dispute. Prior to appointment of Mr. Justice TH Khan, Arbitrator and execution of the Arbitration Agreement the third meeting of the Council Committee on Insurance was held on 21.7.1980 presided over by the Hon'ble Vice President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (page 2 of the, Additional Paper Book-1) and the subject matter was handing, over possession of the Adamjee Court Annex Building to the respondent. The point raised in the meeting that attracts my attention is: "It was felt that such Inter-Ministerial wangling over the  possession of Annex Building should not be  allowed to continue for long and should be decided once and for all." That was the intention of such a higher power Inter-Ministerial Committee. It also took the decision, amongst other, that "(III) The Award of the Arbitrator shall be final and binding on both the parties and be implemented accordingly." And pursuance to decision of the 4th Council Committee meeting held on 19th March, 1981 Mr. Justice TH Khan was appointed sole Arbitrator (vide page 5 of the Additional Paper Book-1) under a letter dated April 16, 1981 for settling the dispute regarding right, title and ownership of the Adamjee Court Annex Building. The Arbitrator entered into reference after due notice to the parties. On the first meeting held on July 18, 1981 the respondent and the appellant appeared through their respective representatives And took time for filing written statement. After filing written statement the arbitration proceedings continued and the parties were heard as many as on 22 days from June 9 to August 10, 1982. The Arbitrator after a protracted hearing and having had gone through the respective written statement and examining the evidence produced made the award on August 29, 1982. He filed the award on 31.10.82 in Court with notice for making it the rule of the Court and Title Suit No. 467 of 1982 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka was instituted. The Court fixed 6.12.82 for return and order but on the prayer of the appellant 24.1.83 was fixed for filing written objection but the same was not filed on that date. Again 24.2.83 was fixed for written statement and order. On that date the respondent prayed for direction on the appellant to serve copy of the written objection and prayer for time to file counter-objection. However, the Court ordered the appellant to serve copy of the written objection on the respondent by 28.4.83. On 28.4.83 the respondent petitioned for rejection of the written objection and the Court directed the appellant to deposit the "value of the property" in award or to furnish security by 22.5.83, in default, on rejection of the written objection the award would be made a rule of the Court. On 22.5.83 as the appellant did not take any step the Court rejected the written objection and decreed the suit ex-parte and made the award rule of the Court without costs. 

 4. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submits, that the award made during pendency of the suits was without jurisdiction as the reference was not in Court under section 21 of the Arbitration Act and the award cannot be made rule of the Court. The award, according to him, is a salish and not an award as no stay order was obtained under section 34 from the Court the arbitration was invalid and the, award is a nullity under section 35 of the Arbitration Act. He cited the decision in the case of LIGH Ariff and others Vs. Bengal Silk Mills Ltd. and another, 1949 Cal. 350 and the case of Zeauddin and others Vs. Abdur Rafique and others, 1952 PAL 66. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, on the other hand, in repelling the contention of Mr. Ahmed refers us to the decision in the case of All India Groundnut Syndicate Ltd, 1945 Born 497 to contend that a party submitting to the Arbitration knowing that the Arbitrator is competent to arbitrate the dispute he should not be allowed to challenge the award on the ground of jurisdiction of the Arbitrator. Let us now consider the decisions cited by the learned Advocates. In the Calcutta case the applicant, Mrs. Aisha Ariff, second wife of Golam Hossain Ariff, instituted a suit praying for declaration that the award published by Ameer Ali, J. umpire, was invalid as there was no submission to arbitration agreement the umpire had no jurisdiction to make the award. In that case dispute arose with regard to certain amount paid to the company, Bengal Silk Mills Ltd. from time to time to help its financial difficulties out of the fund of the partnership firm of which Golam Hossain Ariff and his son through first wife were partners. And on the death of Golan) Hossain Ariff his son Ismail and Aisha filed Suit No. 22161 of 4989 for recovery of money from Bengal Silk. Mills Ltd. The Bengal Silk Mills Co. Ltd. thereafter filed another suit being Suit No. 1 of 1940 against Aisha Ariff, Ismail and Ibrahim who represented the estate of GH Ariff for recovery of Rs. 6 lacs and account. The parties in this suit entered into & written agreement to refer the disputes of the two suits to the arbitration of Mr. JN Basu and Haji Mohammad. Ismail Ariff to make award within a month and agreed that in case of difference of opinion the matter would be referred to Ameer Ali, J. as umpire. In that case there was no order of reference by the Court to Ameer Ali, J as umpire and it was held that award deciding the dispute forming the subject matter of a pending suit without reference in Court was invalid. The case of Zeauddin was on a suit for partition. The parties to the suit agreed to refer the matter in dispute to arbitration. And an Arbitrator was appointed. Under the award made by him the defendant was to deliver vacant possession of the land in dispute to the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs were to pay the cost of litigation. The defendant took objection to the award and the trial court accepted the same but on appeal the appellate Court directed to record the agreement on compromise embodied in the award under Or. 23 r. 3 CPC. The question that fell for consideration before the Court was: whether, when the parties to a suit had referred the matters in dispute between them to arbitration without the intervention, an award could be regarded as an adjustment of the suit and could be recorded as directed by the Appellate Court. The Patna High Court after reviewing many a decision, namely, the decisions in the case of Amar Chand Vs. Anwari Lali Rakshit, 1949 Cal. 608 and the case of the Hari Prashad Vs. Mr. Soogni Devi, 67 IC 123 Vis-a-vis the decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of Manilal Vs. Gokal Das, 1945 Bom. 245 took the view that despite a reference to arbitration and the award the court had no jurisdiction to treat the award as an adjustment of the suit unless all the parties have consented in court to refer to arbitration the matter in dispute between them and to be bound by any award which may be passed. The fact of the case of All India Groundnut Syndicate Ltd. in nutshell, was that the applicant, who wanted to get the award set aside, entered into an agreement with the respondent for supplying a huge quantity of groundnuts. As per clause 10 of the said agreement all disputes which should arise between the parties out of or in connection with the agreement were to be referred to arbitration, in the Bombay City. As usual dispute arose and an interview took place, at the Mount Everest Hotel, at Madras, between the representatives of the parties and an agreement was reached that in all events a fresh agreement would supersede the original agreement. The applicant filed the suit in a court in Bombay raising the dispute whether the agreement, made at the Mount Everest Hotel, was a fresh agreement and if so whether it superseded the original agreement or was a modification or working out of that agreement. It was held by the Court that if a party takes up the proceeding before the arbitration on the assumption that the proceedings were before a competent tribunal he cannot be allowed to argue that the whole proceedings were coram non judice. On facts of the instant case we are to apply the principle laid down in those cases to the case before us. On reference to the agreement in the case before us it appears that it contains a term that award of the arbitrator shall be final and binding on both the parties and all pending suits were to be withdrawn within 7 days. 

 It also appears from record that both the parties before the Arbitrator filed their statements, led evidence and appeared for more than 22 days. The appellant did not pray before the arbitrator for stopping the arbitration proceeding. Rather prayed for passing the award which is evident from the following passage appearing at page 70 of the Additional Paper Book No, II "in the circumstances it is humbly prayed that their Lordships may be graciously pleased to pass an award on the following terms". Therefore, in view of such explicit prayer in an unambiguous language I am led to hold that the appellant submitted to the jurisdiction of the Arbitrator with the knowledge that the Arbitrator was competent to pass the award. Therefore, I am also of the opinion that where the parties submit to the Arbitration without intervention of the court and make a prayer for passing the award such parties cannot be allowed to take objection to the validity of the award on the ground of want of jurisdiction of the Arbitrator on the plea that the reference was not in court. In the case the appellant having had submitted to the arbitration and having had made prayer for passing the award it does not lie in the mouth of the appellant to say that the award suffers from lack of jurisdiction ab initio and on the basis of the award no decree can be passed. In this view of mine I am in respectful agreement with the decisions in the case of All India Groundnuts Syndicate Ltd. and apply the principle laid down therein to the instant case and unable to apply the principle laid down in the cases of 1949 Cal. 350 and 1952 Patna 66 here in the case before us. Even the case before us stands on a stronger footing than the case of Bombay High Court. There was submission under protest before the arbitrator unlike the case before us and the dispute in that case was not a dispute between the two agencies of the same Government like the present one who took decision to settle the dispute "once and for all" on the view that "litigations will not lead to pay fruitful result." Accordingly, the first contention of Mr. Ahmed fails. 

 5. He next contended that the suits not having been withdrawn in terms of the agreement the appellant did not lose the right to challenge the award. Mr. Ahmed again relied upon the decision in the case of Ziauddin and others wherein it has been held that where the parties to a suit referred the matter in dispute between them to the arbitration without intervention of the Court and an award has been made either party to the suit may insist on his right to have the suit tried. This contention has little force. The appellant having had submitted to the arbitration of Mr. Justice TH Khan and prayed for passing the award is estopped to raise this point at this stage more so in view of the terms of the Arbitration Agreement under which the appellant takes upon itself the responsibility to taking necessary step for withdrawal of all pending suits. Thus, the decision in the case of Ziauddin has no manner of application to the facts of the case. 

 7. Placing reliance upon the decision in the case of Kashinathsa Yamosa Kabadi Vs. Narisngsa Bhuskarsa Kabadi, 1961 SC 1077. Mr. Ahmed further argued that in absence of registration of the award under section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act the Court erred in law in decreeing the suit. The contention requires of us to examine the nature of the award. It is to see whether under the award the respondent acquired right, title and interest in the Adamjee Annex Building. In the present case under the award no title accrued, rather it acknowledged what accrued to Adamjee Insurance Co. under the deed of sale executed by Mr. GM Adamjee. The award only acknowledged the true effect of the sale deed and did not create any interest in the immovable property. It is true, as held by the Supreme Court in Kashinathsa, where an award creates or purports to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, title or interest in immovable properties it is compulsorily registerable under section 17 of the Registration Act. But, in my opinion, where under an award no such right, title and interest accrues or is created, declared or assigned the award is not compulsorily registerable. Under the present award as no such right, title and interest accrues or is created or assigned the award is not compulsorily registerable. The principle enunciated in Kashinathsa Yamosa Kabadi, 1961 (SC) 1077 is correct. But in view of my reading of the award and on facts of the present case I am unable to hold that for want of registration the award is invalid and as such the court below committed illegality in decreeing the suit. 

 8. The learned counsel for the appellant further submitted that as there was no arbitration agreement within the meaning of section 2(a) of the Arbitration Act the Court ought to have held that the award was not made by a legally appointed arbitrator. The decision in the case of All India Groundnut Syndicate Ltd. Co. is an answer to the contention and this contention of Mr. Ahmed also fails. 

 10. He further argued that the court failed to hold that the Arbitrator misconducted himself in the proceedings in holding that Mr. GM Adamjee has power to execute the deed of sale on the face of Article 110(2) of the Articles of Association which empowers only the Board of Directors of the Company to sell property. On vesting both M/s Adamjee Sons Ltd. and the Adamjee Insurance Co. is the Government Under PO 16 of 1972 the decision on this contention is only academic one. If the transfer of the Adamjee Annex Building is held illegal it will remain the property of the vendor M/s. Adamjee Sons Ltd. and for that matter it stands vested in the Government and if it is held that the transfer is valid the legal consequences is the same as it becomes the property of the Insurances Co. and for that matter again of the Government in view of PO 16 of 1972. 1 hereafter, to question the authority of Mr. C, Adamjee to transfer the building is an academic without affecting the title of the Government in that building in any way. The contention of Mr. Ahmed, thus, is also untenable. Mr. Ahmed further argued that there being no date fixed for ex-parte hearing of the suit, the ex-parte decree passed on an off date was not legal. In aid of his submission he cited the decisions in the cases of KDH Laboratories Ltd. Vs. Pubali Bank and others, 40 DLR 1, Ails Adamjee Jute Mills Ltd. Vs. Chairman, Third Labour Court and another, 39 DLR 11. As the facts of those cases are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case the principle laid down therein has no application to the facts of the instant case. In the case before us prior to the ex-parte decree made on May 22, 1983 the Court by an order dated April 28, 1983 directed the appellant to deposit the value of the property in award or to furnish security by May 22, 1983 and it also ordered that on the failure to comply with the directions the written objection would be rejected and the award would be made the rule of the Court. I am of the opinion that by the order made on April 28,1983 the suit was fixed for ex-parte hearing on May 22,1983 otherwise the expression the award shall be made a Rule of the Court" will lead to no logical meaning. And in this view of the reading of the said order I hold that the suit was not decreed on an off-date. Mr. Haque also contended that the appellant did not deposit the money or the security as directed by the trial Court. On the failure to deposit the money, he continues to argue, the written objection was rejected. I also find from the record that the appellant did not deposit the amount as directed within the stipulated time. Therefore, this contention of the appellant also fails. 

 11. Mr. Rafiqul Haque cited the case of Banwarilal Garodia Vs. Joylal Hargulal, 1956 Cal. 467 to contend that in order to say that the arbitration proceedings arc invalid notice of legal proceeding is to be given to the Arbitrator and as no such notice was given the proceeding before the Arbitrator and the award made by him cannot be held invalid under section 35 of the Arbitration Act as contended by Mr. Ahmed. I may profitably quote the relevant passage from the report at page 468; "In order to render the arbitration proceedings invalid within the meaning of section 35 of the Act, it is necessary, therefore, that throe very important and distinct conditions must be satisfied namely (1) that a "legal proceeding" must be commenced, (2) secondly, such legal proceeding must be upon the "whole" and not merely part of the subject matter of the reference and (3) thirdly, that a notice of such legal proceeding must be given to the Arbitrators". Being in respectful agreement with the view taken by PB Mukharji, J. I also hold that in order to hold that arbitration proceeding invalid under section 35 of the Act notice of legal proceeding must be given to the Arbitrator and in the case before us that not having been done I cannot accept the contention of the appellant. That was case of setting aside an award on the ground of jurisdiction and misconduct of the arbitrator. In the case before us it is evident from the record that an application was filed before the trial Court for obtaining extension of time to complete arbitration proceeding by the Arbitrator. But nothing was sent to him. On the other hand, the appellant prayed before him to pass the award. 

 13. Before I part with the judgment I am inclined to make some observation on the role of Mi. Md. Siddiqullah, the Principal Officer of the appellant company, in dealing with the case: From the written statement filed in the Trial Court in Title Suit No. 467 of 1982 for setting aside the award (printed at page 182 to 238 of the Paper Book) it appears that the same was sworn by Mr. Siddiqullah. In affidavit of the written objection he stated that he looked after the case and was acquainted with the facts of the case and was a competent person, to depose. This Mr. Siddiqullah was a signatory to the order passed by the Arbitrator on May 27, 1982 wherein it is stated amongst others that a joint application for extension of time was filed before the appropriate court, namely, Subordinate Judge; 3rd Court, Dhaka which was ultimately granted on 24.5.82. The Arbitrator notified the parties on 26.5.82 for the next sitting to be held on May, 1982 at 5-00 PM in the Conference Room of the respondent. Therefore, it was absolutely clear that Mr. Md. Siddiqullah had the knowledge about the arbitration proceeding and the relevant clause of the arbitration agreement to the effect that the award made by the Arbitrator shall be final and be binding upon the parties and the party shall take necessary step within seven days of the execution of the arbitration agreement to withdraw all pending suits from the Court. In spite of such knowledge why Mr. Md. Siddiqullah, the Principal Officer of the appellant M/s. Adamjee Sons Ltd. did not lake step for withdrawal of the cases and dragged the litigation for several years upto the High Court Division resulting in drainage of public money, flouting the decision of a high power Council Committee presided over by the Hon'ble Vice President and attended by the Hon'ble Ministers concerned is mysterious and I know not for whose, benefit he did so. However, this is for the executive department of the Government to see. I also hope that none of the two agencies of the Government should further drag the matter and stop drainage of public money which should be jealously guarded by the public bodies like the present one.
